content: 1. A systematic review published in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine in 2003 (Volume 25, Supplement 2, Pages 129–136) discusses overlapping scopes with other reviews. The review includes studies such as Lee MS, Pittler MH, Shin BC, and Ernst E's systematic review on Tai Chi for osteoporosis, published in Osteoporosis International in 2008 (Volume 19, Issue 2, Pages 139–146). However, this review did not report relevant outcomes. 2. Liu C and Latham N conducted a systematic review on progressive resistance strength training to improve physical function in older adults, published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews in 2009 (Issue 3, Article CD002759). This publication is related to another included review by Liu and Latham (2009). 3. Liu C-J, Shiroy DM, Jones LY, and Clark DO performed a systematic review on the effects of functional training on muscle strength, physical functioning, and activities of daily living in older adults. This review was published in European Review of Aging and Physical Activity in 2014 (Volume 11, Pages 95–106). Eligible trials from this review were included in other reviews already covered in the scope of the current review. 4. Liu-Ambrose T and Donaldson MG explored the role of resistance training programs in exercise and cognition among older adults in a narrative review published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine in 2009 (Volume 43, Issue 1, Pages 25–27). 5. Littbrand H, Stenvall M, and Rosendahl E conducted a systematic review on the applicability and effects of physical exercise on physical and cognitive functions, as well as activities of daily living, among individuals with dementia. This review was published in the American Journal of Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation in 2011 (Volume 90, Issue 6, Pages 495–518). The review focused on residents in long-term care facilities. 6. The evidence profile for mobility loss was developed as part of the iCOPE guidelines by the World Health Organization. The search strategy included databases such as MEDLINE, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Library. The search was limited to randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and clinical trials involving older adults (aged 65 and above). The search excluded animal studies, non-English publications, conference proceedings, and commentaries. 7. A PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) flow diagram was used to document the review process for mobility loss. A total of 325 records were screened after duplicates were removed. Of these, 20 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility, and 9 were excluded because the trials they cited were already included in other reviews. Reasons for exclusion of records included population mismatch (120), intervention mismatch (78), comparison issues (5), irrelevant outcomes (90), duplication (9), non-English publications (1), conference proceedings (1), and commentaries (1). This detailed analysis highlights the systematic approach taken to evaluate the effects of exercise interventions on physical and cognitive functions in older adults, with a focus on evidence-based practices and rigorous inclusion criteria.
